GLOBAL WELLNESS INDEX

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In a recent global health wellness study, South Africa was ranked as the unhealthiest country in the world. How do we as a nation turn this situation around?

Unique Selling Point:
In what is called to be the most comprehensive global health index of its sort using the the most recent statistics from the World Health Organisation, The World Happiness Report and other public data, British economy firm, Bloomsbury Economists compiled a report from 191 countries using 10 health measurements - healthy life expectancy, blood pressure, blood glucose (the risk of diabetes), obesity, depression, happiness, alcohol use, tobacco use, inactivity (too little exercise) and government spending on healthcare.

South Africa was ranked stone last out of the 191 countries - as the unhealthiest country in 2019.

Summary:
-IT CALCULATED A RATIO TO ASSES HOW CLOSE EACH COUNTRY IS TO THE BEST SCORE OVERALL - THE WORST SCORE BEING 0, WHILE THE BEST SCORE BEING 1
-WITH A SCORE OF 0,28, SOUTH AFRICA WAS RANKED AS THE UNHEALTHIEST COUNTRY IN THE WORLD IN 2019 - WHILE CANADA CAME OUT TOPS
-SOUTH AFRICA ESPECIALLY SCORED POORLY IN INACTIVITY, LIFE EXPECTANCY, ALCOHOL USE, AND OBESITY (IN THE 0.0 CIRCLE) - THEN BLOOD PRESSURE, HAPPINESS (IN 0,2 CIRCLE) - THEN DEPRESSION AND TOBACCO USE (IN 0.4 CIRCLE) - WITH THE BEST SCORE IN THE 0,6 MARGIN IN GOVERNMENT SPENDING ON HEALTHCARE.
-SOUTH AFRICANS HAVE A 26% PROBABILITY - WITH OTHER WORDS ONE QUARTER OF OUR POPULATION = 15 MILLION OF OUR CURRENT POPULATION OF 57,9 MILLION) ARE LIKELY TO DIE FROM CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE, CANCER, DIABETES, OR CHRONIC RESPIRATORY DISEASE BETWEEN THE AGES 30 TO 70.
-ALMOST ALL OF THESE DISEASES COULD DIRECTLY BE LINKED TO AN UNHEALTHY LIFESTYLE WHICH WAS MEASURED DURING THE HEALTH INDEX - INACTIVITY, ALCOHOL USE, OBESITY, BLOOD PRESSURE, DEPRESSION, TOBACCO USE…
-ANOTHER RATHER SHOCKING FINDING FROM THE WORLD HEALTH ORGANISATION IN ITS 2018 REPORT IS THAT 28% OF ADULTS AND 20% OF CHILDREN IN SOUTH AFRICA WERE OBESE - IT IS THE HIGHEST OBESITY RATE AMONG SUB-SAHARAN AFRICAN COUNTRIES.
-IN TERMS OF LIFE EXPECTANCY, 2018 DATA FROM THE WHO INDICATES MOST BABIES BORN IN SOUTH AFRICA THIS YEAR WON'T SEE THE 22ND CENTURY, THE YEAR 2100.
-THE CURRENT LIFE EXPECTANCY IN SOUTH AFRICA IS ONLY 63,6 YEARS
-ALTHOUGH THE WHO FOUND THAT SA HAS ONE OF THE HIGHEST RATES OF UNIVERSAL HEALTH COVERAGE ON THE CONTINENT, WITH 97% OF BIRTHS ATTENDED BY SKILLED HEALTH PERSONNEL, THE REPORT SHOWS THAT TB, HIV AND THE OTHER NON-COMMUNABLE DISEASES SUCH AS CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE, CANCER, DIABETES, OR CHRONIC RESPIRATORY DISEASE ARE TAKING A MASSIVE TOLL ON OUR COUNTRY'S HEALTH


Further information:
-ALCOHOL USE:THE WORLD HEALTH ORGANISATION HAS ALSO RECENTLY BROUGHT OUT A REPORT RANKING SOUTH AFRICA AS THE SIXTH DRUNKEST COUNTRY IN THE WORLD
-THE REPORT USE A SCALE OF ONE TO FIVE TO RANK A COUNTRY'S RISKY DRINKING PATTERNS, WITH ONE BEING THE LOWEST AND FIVE THE HIGHEST. ONLY RUSSIA AND UKRAINE SCORED FIVE, WITH SOUTH AFRICA SCORING FOUR.
-THE WHO STATES THAT 7% OF SOUTH AFRICANS SUFFER FROM DISORDERS DUE TO DANGEROUS DRINKING, 2% OF SOUTH AFRICANS ARE PHYSIOLOGICALLY AND PSYCHOLOGICALLY DEFENDANT ON ALCOHOL, AND THAT 6% OF ALL DEATHS WITHIN SOUTH AFRICA ARE SOLELY BECAUSE OF ALCOHOL.

-IF THERE IS A PROBLEM OF ALCOHOL USE, THERE IS MOST PROBABLY A PROBLEM WITH PSYCHOLOGICAL ILLNESSES LIKE DEPRESSION - 11 OUT OF EVERY 100 000 PEOPLE COMMIT SUICIDE
-ACCORDING THE MARCH 2019 WORLD HAPPINESS REPORT, SOUTH AFRICA RANKED 106TH OUT OF 156 COUNTRY.



But how do we turn this around?

As a nation, we don't just have to sit back and say: Okay, well, this is how we fared, we'll see what the stats say next year.
The sooner we do something about it, the healthier the nation will get.

An unhealthy lifestyle can be turned around.
If a person is overweight, he can lose weight by adopting the right lifestyle - eating the right food and starting to exercise.
Parents and teachers can start to teach these principles to children at school level already.

It is not necessary that 26% of the SA population should die from noncommunicable diseases such as diabetes, high blood pressure, treatable cancers, and respiratory diseases that are very treatable.

Our experts will speak to the stats and the facts, but also tell us how it is possible to turn the situation around.
Our case studies tell inspirational stories of how they turned their own lives around.

Press Release:


Turning SA’s Poor Health Around

Drawing on reports from the World Health Organisation, World Happiness Report and public health data, the 2019 global Indigo Wellness Index ranked South Africa as the unhealthiest country in the world. From life expectancy to blood pressure, obesity, happiness, and government spending on healthcare, several wellness indicators applied to 191 countries showed us performing the worst. What will it take for South Africans to turn this picture on its head in years to come? Carte Blanche explores the options for our unhealthy society.

Producer: Este de Klerk

Presenter: Claire Mawisa

Script:


GLOBAL WELLNESS INDEX SCRIPT FINAL

PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK
PRESENTER: CLAIRE MAWISA
BROADCAST DATE:

VO: At the age of 25, Ryno Marx is the picture of good health as he trains on the Sea Point promenade in Cape Town.
But it was only three years ago that he was so overweight, he could barely go for a few minutes' walk.

RYNO MARX: From school, varsity, stressed a lot. I would eat a lot. I would see exercise as a… "I don't have time for that." My team would say now I'm half the man I used to be.

VO: Ryno's heaviest low-point in 2016 was 135kg with a body mass index - or BMI - of 42.
BMI measures height in relation to weight - with a healthy BMI ranging between 18 and 25.
With his at 42, Ryno was classified morbidly obese.
A friend's gentle nudging helped him see the light.

RYNO MARX: he mentioned - in my studies, because I take it so seriously, and then he kind of diverted that conversation in the way of: ou can also focus that mindset into getting healthy. Then it hit me that I'm actually so far down the wrong path that this is actually my friend' and family's way of telling me, "We need to get you on the right path."

VO: Ryno changed his life incrementally - he began exercising and changed his eating habits - just one step at a time. But, gradually he lost 39% of his weight over three years.

RYNO MARX: I'm currently on 84kg, so just a weight-loss of just over 50kg.

VO: Taking small steps towards radical change is the secret says dietitian and lecturer in nutrition at the University of Cape Town, Gabriel Eksteen.

GABRIEL EKSTEEN: You don't become overweight within a couple of weeks. So, when we suddenly want you to change and put you on a diet your body aggressively fights against that.

VO: Despite France's decadent diet of rich deserts and pastries, only 19% of French people are considered obese. In South Africa the number jumps to 70% of women and 39% of men, making us the most obese country in Sub-Saharan Africa.

CLAIRE LINK: It may seem that South Africans are keen on physical activity. Many are seen walking and jogging on promenades across the country. But in a recent study we have been found to be some of the most inactive people on the planet.

VO: Inactivity and levels of obesity were two of the ten measures in a new global health index to determine the healthiest and unhealthiest countries in the world. Life expectancy, happiness level, blood pressure, depression, alcohol and tobacco use and government spending on healthcare were also measured.

Out of 191 countries, South Africa was ranked the unhealthiest in the world.
So, how did we manage to reach this low point?
Naturopath, dr Karen Morris.

DR KAREN MORRIS: in effect we've got stone-age genes and a very modern industrialized diet and there's just a very serious mismatch.

VO: Dr Morris has noticed that patients live such fast paced lives that feeling fatigued, bloated or having constant headaches becomes their new normal.

DR KAREN MORRIS: People are working quite hard sometimes to be healthy, but Our gut can only be as healthy as the food that we put into our mouth.

VO: According to the World Health Organisation, the average global life expectancy is 72 years.
In South Africa, it's 63 years - while in war-torn Iraq it's 69. That's compared to the Japanese who on average live to 84.
Our low life expectancy is directly linked to lifestyle diseases we're likely to die from, such as diabetes, hypertension, cancers and heart- and lung-illnesses.

GABRIEL EKSTEEN: As a general rule, we say that 80% of those diseases can be prevented if we acted early and acted decisively.

VO: But it's not always so easy, says 29-year old Gabby Abrahamse who describes her battle with obesity as an "a lifelong rollercoaster ride".

CLAIRE REVERSAL TO GABBY: You have gotten help along the way? Did it work?

GABBY ABRAHAMSE: nope. Unless if you have a private chef that's going to be cooking these meals and packing it for you, it's impossible to do.

VO: We featured Gabby in a Carte Blanche story on childhood obesity in 2003 when she was just 13 years old.

GABBY ABRAHAMSE: In matric I had lost weight and then I was at my goal.

VO: But within the next five years, she gained 50kg and pushed the scale at a 130.

GABBY ABRAHAMSE: And then I started working, and I started eating my money.

GABRIEL EKSTEEN: The longer you have obesity, the more likely you are to get the secondary effects - the diabetes, high blood pressure, etc

VO: This became Gabby's fate - even though she's managed to lose 30kg again since 2014 and now weighs just under a 100.

GABBY ABRAHAMSE: I'm a bit hypertensive. I'm not even 30. I also feel like it's hereditary.

VO: But experts believe it is possible to reverse early-stage diabetes and hypertension.

DR KAREN MORRIS: Genes loads the gun but the environment pulls the trigger.

GABRIEL EKSTEEN: If people lose about 15% of their body weight and maintain that weight loss, they can remain in remission from their diabetes.

VO: Dr Morris says the simplest adjustment to make is to drastically change our shopping habits.

DR MORRIS: Go into certain parts of the supermarket almost exclusively and other areas almost never.

VO: According to Dr Morris one should only shop from aisles with fresh produce like fruit, veg, diary, meat, chicken and fish; and unprocessed grains like lentils and beans.
Avoid sugary cereals, processed foods and bread.

DR MORRIS: If you've got access to good bread the way it used to be made then it's different. Rather don't eat modern bread and get- the equivalent of sustenance - from your dried peas, beans, lentils.

VO: We live in the fast lane where time is of the essence, and food on the go is often more convenient.

But everything eventually adds up - and an unhealthy gut has been linked to mental health illnesses like depression.

DR MORRIS: There's actually more serotonin that's made in our gut than in our brain. So, if we are eating a diet that's feeding the non-beneficial bacteria, those bacteria end up making us feel bad.

VO: The high level of depression in our country is evident in our ranking according to the World Happiness Report. Out of a total of 156 countries, South Africa ranks a sad 106th.

JUDGE EBERHARD BERTELSMANN: Because we have all these fractures in our society, stress leads to the use of either tranquilisers and to drink to relax.

VO: Retired High Court Judge Eberhard Bertelsmann spent a career under pressure in the fast lane. But he's recently celebrated 33 years of sobriety. His doctor at the time had prescribed highly addictive anti-anxiety meds which Judge Bertelsmann became dependant on. One addiction led to another and he became an alcoholic.

JUDGE BERTELSMANN: I was very close in my depression to considering suicide. And the critical point for any start of rehabilitation, is for the addict to realise that he's lost control.

VO: After a successful stint in rehab, Bertelsmann became a senior advocate, then magistrate and retired as a High Court Judge in 2016 after 16 years on the bench. Since his own rehabilitation, he's counselled thousands of addicts in their own fight to overcome the disease.

JUDGE BERTELSMANN: with it came the need to tell people that there were second chances. Once you are addicted, you remain addicted, but you can deal with it.

VO: And the experts agree that it's in grabbing hold of second chances that we need to find the solutions to change our country's health and wellbeing prospects.

GABRIEL EKSTEEN: our healthcare system is battling all these conditions. We have to fix the problems we have, whether that is HIV or heart disease, strokes, and not enough money, budget-wise, is put into preventing in the first place.


- End -

PROMO 1:11"

A new global health index has rated South Africa the world's most obese, depressed and inactive nation.

GABRIEL EKSTEEN: if we acted early and acted decisively, most of these diseases can be prevented.

PROMO 2: 11"

South Africa has been ranked the unhealthiest country in the world by a new global wellness index.

DR KAREN MORRIS: in effect we've got stone-age genes and a very modern industrialized diet and there's just a very serious mismatch.

PROMO 3: 11"

We're rated the unhealthiest country in the world - What can South Africans do to change our current low life expectancy due to prevalent lifestyle diseases?

From life expectancy to blood pressure, obesity, happiness, and government spending on healthcare, several wellness indicators applied to 191 countries showed us performing the worst. What will it take for South Africans to turn this picture on its head in years to come? Carte Blanche explores the options for our unhealthy society. Producer: Este de Klerk Presenter: Claire Mawisa Script: GLOBAL WELLNESS INDEX SCRIPT FINAL PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK PRESENTER: CLAIRE MAWISA BROADCAST DATE: VO: At the age of 25, Ryno Marx is the picture of good health as he trains on the Sea Point promenade in Cape Town. But it was only three years ago that he was so overweight, he could barely go for a few minutes' walk. RYNO MARX: From school, varsity, stressed a lot. I would eat a lot. I would see exercise as a… "I don't have time for that." My team would say now I'm half the man I used to be. VO: Ryno's heaviest low-point in 2016 was 135kg with a body mass index - or BMI - of 42. BMI measures height in relation to weight - with a healthy BMI ranging between 18 and 25. With his at 42, Ryno was classified morbidly obese. A friend's gentle nudging helped him see the light. RYNO MARX: he mentioned - in my studies, because I take it so seriously, and then he kind of diverted that conversation in the way of: ou can also focus that mindset into getting healthy. Then it hit me that I'm actually so far down the wrong path that this is actually my friend' and family's way of telling me, "We need to get you on the right path." VO: Ryno changed his life incrementally - he began exercising and changed his eating habits - just one step at a time. But, gradually he lost 39% of his weight over three years. RYNO MARX: I'm currently on 84kg, so just a weight-loss of just over 50kg. VO: Taking small steps towards radical change is the secret says dietitian and lecturer in nutrition at the University of Cape Town, Gabriel Eksteen. GABRIEL EKSTEEN: You don't become overweight within a couple of weeks. So, when we suddenly want you to change and put you on a diet your body aggressively fights against that. VO: Despite France's decadent diet of rich deserts and pastries, only 19% of French people are considered obese. In South Africa the number jumps to 70% of women and 39% of men, making us the most obese country in Sub-Saharan Africa. CLAIRE LINK: It may seem that South Africans are keen on physical activity. Many are seen walking and jogging on promenades across the country. But in a recent study we have been found to be some of the most inactive people on the planet. VO: Inactivity and levels of obesity were two of the ten measures in a new global health index to determine the healthiest and unhealthiest countries in the world. Life expectancy, happiness level, blood pressure, depression, alcohol and tobacco use and government spending on healthcare were also measured. Out of 191 countries, South Africa was ranked the unhealthiest in the world. So, how did we manage to reach this low point? Naturopath, dr Karen Morris. DR KAREN MORRIS: in effect we've got stone-age genes and a very modern industrialized diet and there's just a very serious mismatch. VO: Dr Morris has noticed that patients live such fast paced lives that feeling fatigued, bloated or having constant headaches becomes their new normal. DR KAREN MORRIS: People are working quite hard sometimes to be healthy, but Our gut can only be as healthy as the food that we put into our mouth. VO: According to the World Health Organisation, the average global life expectancy is 72 years. In South Africa, it's 63 years - while in war-torn Iraq it's 69. That's compared to the Japanese who on average live to 84. Our low life expectancy is directly linked to lifestyle diseases we're likely to die from, such as diabetes, hypertension, cancers and heart- and lung-illnesses. GABRIEL EKSTEEN: As a general rule, we say that 80% of those diseases can be prevented if we acted early and acted decisively. VO: But it's not always so easy, says 29-year old Gabby Abrahamse who describes her battle with obesity as an "a lifelong rollercoaster ride". CLAIRE REVERSAL TO GABBY: You have gotten help along the way? Did it work? GABBY ABRAHAMSE: nope. Unless if you have a private chef that's going to be cooking these meals and packing it for you, it's impossible to do. VO: We featured Gabby in a Carte Blanche story on childhood obesity in 2003 when she was just 13 years old. GABBY ABRAHAMSE: In matric I had lost weight and then I was at my goal. VO: But within the next five years, she gained 50kg and pushed the scale at a 130. GABBY ABRAHAMSE: And then I started working, and I started eating my money. GABRIEL EKSTEEN: The longer you have obesity, the more likely you are to get the secondary effects - the diabetes, high blood pressure, etc VO: This became Gabby's fate - even though she's managed to lose 30kg again since 2014 and now weighs just under a 100. GABBY ABRAHAMSE: I'm a bit hypertensive. I'm not even 30. I also feel like it's hereditary. VO: But experts believe it is possible to reverse early-stage diabetes and hypertension. DR KAREN MORRIS: Genes loads the gun but the environment pulls the trigger. GABRIEL EKSTEEN: If people lose about 15% of their body weight and maintain that weight loss, they can remain in remission from their diabetes. VO: Dr Morris says the simplest adjustment to make is to drastically change our shopping habits. DR MORRIS: Go into certain parts of the supermarket almost exclusively and other areas almost never. VO: According to Dr Morris one should only shop from aisles with fresh produce like fruit, veg, diary, meat, chicken and fish; and unprocessed grains like lentils and beans. Avoid sugary cereals, processed foods and bread. DR MORRIS: If you've got access to good bread the way it used to be made then it's different. Rather don't eat modern bread and get- the equivalent of sustenance - from your dried peas, beans, lentils. VO: We live in the fast lane where time is of the essence, and food on the go is often more convenient. But everything eventually adds up - and an unhealthy gut has been linked to mental health illnesses like depression. DR MORRIS: There's actually more serotonin that's made in our gut than in our brain. So, if we are eating a diet that's feeding the non-beneficial bacteria, those bacteria end up making us feel bad. VO: The high level of depression in our country is evident in our ranking according to the World Happiness Report. Out of a total of 156 countries, South Africa ranks a sad 106th. JUDGE EBERHARD BERTELSMANN: Because we have all these fractures in our society, stress leads to the use of either tranquilisers and to drink to relax. VO: Retired High Court Judge Eberhard Bertelsmann spent a career under pressure in the fast lane. But he's recently celebrated 33 years of sobriety. His doctor at the time had prescribed highly addictive anti-anxiety meds which Judge Bertelsmann became dependant on. One addiction led to another and he became an alcoholic. JUDGE BERTELSMANN: I was very close in my depression to considering suicide. And the critical point for any start of rehabilitation, is for the addict to realise that he's lost control. VO: After a successful stint in rehab, Bertelsmann became a senior advocate, then magistrate and retired as a High Court Judge in 2016 after 16 years on the bench. Since his own rehabilitation, he's counselled thousands of addicts in their own fight to overcome the disease. JUDGE BERTELSMANN: with it came the need to tell people that there were second chances. Once you are addicted, you remain addicted, but you can deal with it. VO: And the experts agree that it's in grabbing hold of second chances that we need to find the solutions to change our country's health and wellbeing prospects. GABRIEL EKSTEEN: our healthcare system is battling all these conditions. We have to fix the problems we have, whether that is HIV or heart disease, strokes, and not enough money, budget-wise, is put into preventing in the first place. - End - PROMOS PROMO 1:11" A new global health index has rated South Africa the world's most obese, depressed and inactive nation. GABRIEL EKSTEEN: if we acted early and acted decisively, most of these diseases can be prevented. PROMO 2: 11" South Africa has been ranked the unhealthiest country in the world by a new global wellness index. DR KAREN MORRIS: in effect we've got stone-age genes and a very modern industrialized diet and there's just a very serious mismatch. PROMO 3: 11" We're rated the unhealthiest country in the world - What can South Africans do to change our current low life expectancy due to prevalent lifestyle diseases?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): In a recent global health wellness study, South Africa was ranked as the unhealthiest country in the world. How do we as a nation turn this situation around?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In what is called to be the most comprehensive global health index of its sort using the the most recent statistics from the World Health Organisation, The World Happiness Report and other public data, British economy firm, Bloomsbury Economists compiled a report from 191 countries using 10 health measurements - healthy life expectancy, blood pressure, blood glucose (the risk of diabetes), obesity, depression, happiness, alcohol use, tobacco use, inactivity (too little exercise) and government spending on healthcare. South Africa was ranked stone last out of the 191 countries - as the unhealthiest country in 2019.
metadata.Summary: -IT CALCULATED A RATIO TO ASSES HOW CLOSE EACH COUNTRY IS TO THE BEST SCORE OVERALL - THE WORST SCORE BEING 0, WHILE THE BEST SCORE BEING 1 -WITH A SCORE OF 0,28, SOUTH AFRICA WAS RANKED AS THE UNHEALTHIEST COUNTRY IN THE WORLD IN 2019 - WHILE CANADA CAME OUT TOPS -SOUTH AFRICA ESPECIALLY SCORED POORLY IN INACTIVITY, LIFE EXPECTANCY, ALCOHOL USE, AND OBESITY (IN THE 0.0 CIRCLE) - THEN BLOOD PRESSURE, HAPPINESS (IN 0,2 CIRCLE) - THEN DEPRESSION AND TOBACCO USE (IN 0.4 CIRCLE) - WITH THE BEST SCORE IN THE 0,6 MARGIN IN GOVERNMENT SPENDING ON HEALTHCARE. -SOUTH AFRICANS HAVE A 26% PROBABILITY - WITH OTHER WORDS ONE QUARTER OF OUR POPULATION = 15 MILLION OF OUR CURRENT POPULATION OF 57,9 MILLION) ARE LIKELY TO DIE FROM CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE, CANCER, DIABETES, OR CHRONIC RESPIRATORY DISEASE BETWEEN THE AGES 30 TO 70. -ALMOST ALL OF THESE DISEASES COULD DIRECTLY BE LINKED TO AN UNHEALTHY LIFESTYLE WHICH WAS MEASURED DURING THE HEALTH INDEX - INACTIVITY, ALCOHOL USE, OBESITY, BLOOD PRESSURE, DEPRESSION, TOBACCO USE… -ANOTHER RATHER SHOCKING FINDING FROM THE WORLD HEALTH ORGANISATION IN ITS 2018 REPORT IS THAT 28% OF ADULTS AND 20% OF CHILDREN IN SOUTH AFRICA WERE OBESE - IT IS THE HIGHEST OBESITY RATE AMONG SUB-SAHARAN AFRICAN COUNTRIES. -IN TERMS OF LIFE EXPECTANCY, 2018 DATA FROM THE WHO INDICATES MOST BABIES BORN IN SOUTH AFRICA THIS YEAR WON'T SEE THE 22ND CENTURY, THE YEAR 2100. -THE CURRENT LIFE EXPECTANCY IN SOUTH AFRICA IS ONLY 63,6 YEARS -ALTHOUGH THE WHO FOUND THAT SA HAS ONE OF THE HIGHEST RATES OF UNIVERSAL HEALTH COVERAGE ON THE CONTINENT, WITH 97% OF BIRTHS ATTENDED BY SKILLED HEALTH PERSONNEL, THE REPORT SHOWS THAT TB, HIV AND THE OTHER NON-COMMUNABLE DISEASES SUCH AS CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE, CANCER, DIABETES, OR CHRONIC RESPIRATORY DISEASE ARE TAKING A MASSIVE TOLL ON OUR COUNTRY'S HEALTH
metadata.Further information: -ALCOHOL USE:THE WORLD HEALTH ORGANISATION HAS ALSO RECENTLY BROUGHT OUT A REPORT RANKING SOUTH AFRICA AS THE SIXTH DRUNKEST COUNTRY IN THE WORLD -THE REPORT USE A SCALE OF ONE TO FIVE TO RANK A COUNTRY'S RISKY DRINKING PATTERNS, WITH ONE BEING THE LOWEST AND FIVE THE HIGHEST. ONLY RUSSIA AND UKRAINE SCORED FIVE, WITH SOUTH AFRICA SCORING FOUR. -THE WHO STATES THAT 7% OF SOUTH AFRICANS SUFFER FROM DISORDERS DUE TO DANGEROUS DRINKING, 2% OF SOUTH AFRICANS ARE PHYSIOLOGICALLY AND PSYCHOLOGICALLY DEFENDANT ON ALCOHOL, AND THAT 6% OF ALL DEATHS WITHIN SOUTH AFRICA ARE SOLELY BECAUSE OF ALCOHOL. -IF THERE IS A PROBLEM OF ALCOHOL USE, THERE IS MOST PROBABLY A PROBLEM WITH PSYCHOLOGICAL ILLNESSES LIKE DEPRESSION - 11 OUT OF EVERY 100 000 PEOPLE COMMIT SUICIDE -ACCORDING THE MARCH 2019 WORLD HAPPINESS REPORT, SOUTH AFRICA RANKED 106TH OUT OF 156 COUNTRY. But how do we turn this around? As a nation, we don't just have to sit back and say: Okay, well, this is how we fared, we'll see what the stats say next year. The sooner we do something about it, the healthier the nation will get. An unhealthy lifestyle can be turned around. If a person is overweight, he can lose weight by adopting the right lifestyle - eating the right food and starting to exercise. Parents and teachers can start to teach these principles to children at school level already. It is not necessary that 26% of the SA population should die from noncommunicable diseases such as diabetes, high blood pressure, treatable cancers, and respiratory diseases that are very treatable. Our experts will speak to the stats and the facts, but also tell us how it is possible to turn the situation around. Our case studies tell inspirational stories of how they turned their own lives around.
